## THE FAILURE STORY

The v5/v7 refactor was tightly coupled—v5 defined shared schemas and import paths, v7 consumed them. The 43 commits came from 10 worktrees running in parallel, each with a complete local picture but no global view of dependencies. When merging to main chronologically (July 15–18 order), a v7 consumer commit (July 16) landed before the v5 provider commit (July 18) it depended on. Python import resolution broke silently; the symbol simply didn't exist yet on main. Subsequent commits in the queue landed on top of broken code. By the time the actual v5 definition arrived four commits later, downstream code had already layered invalid assumptions on top—assignments to undefined names, circular imports where v7 now imported v5 which imported utilities that now imported v7. Each worktree's tests passed locally (they were testing their own snapshot). Main was broken in the middle, in a state no worktree had ever actually validated. The CB light integration assumed clean boundaries; instead, system_v5 and system_v7 were now entangled on the main branch. Rolling back meant untangling all 43 commits because the merged state had become canonical—other branches had already started depending on the shape of main, even though main was incoherent.

## THE UNDERLYING ASSUMPTION

That merge order (chronological by commit date) preserves functional dependencies, and that locally-passing tests in isolated worktrees guarantee the merged result will be coherent.

## EARLY WARNING SIGNS

1. **Import errors bloom on main within 2–3 commits of the merge sequence.** A commit lands, CI reports undefined symbols or circular imports from system_v5 or system_v7—symptoms that say "a dependency hasn't arrived yet," not "this code is wrong."

2. **A worktree's test suite passes locally; the same test fails on main.** The test itself is fine; the imported module literally does not exist in main's current state because its defining commit is still in the queue upstream.
